https://hungarytoday.hu/european-energy-.text: European Energy Giant Expands into the Domestic Solar Power Market The Greek PPC Group is continuing its growth strategy by entering the Hungarian market through the acquisition of a major renewable energy project. The investment is part of a €24 billion strategic plan aimed at transforming the company into a leading energy player in Central and Southeastern Europe. According to a company statement , PPC Group, through its wholly owned subsidiary PPC Renewables, has reached an agreement with the Greenvolt Group. The deal involves the integration of an operational photovoltaic (solar) park with a capacity of 57.5 megawatts (MW) into PPC’s generation portfolio. The solar power plant is located near Királyegyháza in Baranya County, southwestern Hungary, and has been supplying solar electricity to the grid since July 2024. With an expected operating lifetime of more than 30 years, the project represents a long-term strategic asset for the company. A key advantage of the transaction is its financial stability. The solar power plant operates under a government-backed fixed-price power purchase agreement (PPA) with 25 years remaining. This provides PPC Group with protection against volatility in international electricity markets. Beyond the solar park itself, the agreement with Greenvolt Group also includes the right to acquire a 49 MW battery energy storage system (BESS) currently under development in the same region. The combination of renewable generation and energy storage is considered essential for maintaining the stability of modern electricity grids. The expansion into Hungary is not an isolated project but a key component of PPC Group’s new strategic growth plan for 2026–2030. At the heart of this strategy is a €24 billion investment program designed to double the company’s total installed generation capacity over the coming years. The objective is to build a unified, resilient clean energy platform extending geographically from Greece across the Balkans to Central Europe. Hungary offers ideal conditions for this expansion. The country is regarded as one of Europe’s most attractive growth markets for renewable energy. The Hungarian government is pursuing a comprehensive energy transition program that aims to increase the country’s installed photovoltaic capacity to 12 gigawatts (GW) by 2030. This expansion is supported by a stable regulatory framework aligned with European Union directives, providing investors with the planning certainty needed for large-scale infrastructure projects. Entering the Hungarian market makes our strategy for the new phase of expansion in Central and Southeastern Europe tangible,” said Konstantinos Mavros, Deputy CEO of PPC Group for Renewable Energy. Photo: Pixabay “As part of our strategy through 2030, we are entering new markets such as Hungary, Poland, and Slovakia, where we aim to develop a total of 2.2 GW of renewable energy and energy storage capacity. With this new photovoltaic project, we are integrating a highly efficient asset into our portfolio, expanding our geographic footprint, and building a resilient regional platform for clean energy,” he added. PPC Group’s long-term vision involves a far-reaching transformation. By 2030, 45% of the group’s installed generation capacity is expected to be located outside its home market of Greece. To achieve this, the company is pursuing both technological and geographic diversification. Its target energy mix will encompass the full range of modern technologies, including solar, wind, hydropower, flexible natural gas power plants, and advanced energy storage systems. Solar energy reaches record levels in the national electricity system, outperforming major European peers. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck86.text: Figure caption, Flash flood washes building complex in central Nepal By Navin Singh Khadka Environment correspondent, BBC World Service Published 9 hours ago A major river in Nepal has flooded, sweeping away houses, bridges and damaging a part of hydropower station, authorities have said. Around 50 people have been rescued from along the bank of the Budhi Gandaki River in the central Gorkha district, the army confirmed. No casualties have been reported yet, however five people are missing. A video of the flood shows the moment raging waters sweep down a valley and wash away an entire building complex. Nepal is on high alert and still trying to recover from catastrophic floods that hit its border towns with Tibet two months ago, leaving more than 1,400 people dead and thousands missing. Sunday's flood tore through the Gorkha district as children and communities prepared to mark the first day of the Dashain festival, a major moment in the Nepali calendar. Families have been forced to flee their homes, with many facing uncertainty over where they will find safe shelter and access to essential supplies. The flood swept away about a dozen houses and several suspension bridges, while a hydroelectric project was damaged, carrying some of the construction equipment away, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said. Within a couple of hours, the river's water levels at one location had risen from two metres (6ft 5in) to nearly 8.5m (27ft 9in), officials said. Binod Parajuli, a meteorologist who works with the Nepalese government, said: "Our hydrological station was swept away and we are not getting any data from that location." However, experts say the debris-flow is much smaller and travelled more slowly than the devastating flash floods in August. What caused the latest flood is still unclear. Some say a landslide may have blocked the river or its tributary for some time, causing the dammed water to burst out, while others say locals upstream saw an ice-avalanche. Save the Children is mobilising an emergency team to respond to Sunday's flood. "Children's lives have been ripped apart in an instant yet again", the charity's director in Nepal, Tara Chettry, said. "We are yet to see the full scale of the damage, but they may have lost their homes, schools and communities. Many children in Gorkha will still be in shock and distress after the mega floods in August, barely having a chance to get back on their feet." The Budhi Gandaki is a tributary of the Trishuli river, downstream from another tributary where a glacier collapse caused the previous disaster.
